summary:
West Bengal stands under India's national framework. Parliament's Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill of March 2026 replaced the 2019 law's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals, so trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist, while the government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018 and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, read to cover gender identity, but same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available.

Criminal-law protection weakened nationally in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code.

The land border is a documented exposure point. South Dinajpur police arrested a Bangladeshi transgender person from Sirajganj district, named in reporting as Ali Mondal aka Bijli Mondal, together with the e-rickshaw driver who brought her across the border, on allegations of infiltrating India. Trans presentation operated as the basis for an illegal-entry charge rather than as identity, and the encounter was driven by state actors, which is the mechanism a foreign visitor transiting the border would meet.

Gender-checking conduct by security personnel is recorded in the provincial capital. On 18 August 2024 a group of trans women heading to RG Kar Medical College filed an FIR alleging that a Railway Protection Force constable at Rabindra Sadan metro station groped one of them to check her gender and made inappropriate remarks. Metro Railway and the Railway Protection Force denied the allegations and counter-filed an FIR against the group, while footage showed the trans woman in tears.

Crime recorded against trans people in West Bengal is detectable rather than absent. Of the seven Transgender Persons Act cases registered nationally in 2021, three were registered in West Bengal, the highest count that year alongside Assam and Kerala. National totals remain very small, 20 cases across 2019 to 2023, which the reporting attributes to police-registration bias rather than to low incidence, and a 2025 survey put prevalence at 27.2% physical violence and 22.3% sexual violence.
tangentialFactors:
West Bengal's three Transgender Persons Act cases in 2021 placed it level with Assam and Kerala at the top of a national table whose totals are themselves very low. Any comparison drawn from those counts is distorted by the registration bias the reporting identifies, so a small number here does not establish a lower level of violence than in states recording fewer cases.

Checkpoint friction is documented across India rather than confined to this state. Transgender people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam recounted degrading treatment in custody in interviews recorded in June 2024; at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 in November 2024, CISF personnel stopped an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, although she presented a PAN card; and passport authorities have required a trans applicant to sit a medical examination, with the Allahabad High Court granting relief in February 2026.

The courts remain the strongest protection machinery nationally. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, delivered by Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, issued sweeping guidelines covering police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy, and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. The UK Home Office country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic. No West Bengal-specific judicial intervention appears in the sources.

Recognition narrowed for everyone in March 2026, so document and identity claims made at West Bengal checkpoints rest on a national scheme that excludes many trans and non-binary people, whatever the state's own practice.
localsOnly:
West Bengal is one of the 12 states and union territories that notified a transgender welfare board, according to an RTI investigation published on 5 November 2024. Nationally the majority of boards have held fewer than one meeting per year since their creation, and the 17 existing boards are described as mostly running rudderless without a policy framework, compliance mechanism, or any power, with several functioning as non-transparent bodies that diffuse demands instead of serving trans people. West Bengal's constituted welfare board operates without a functioning policy framework.

Residents can register complaints under the Transgender Persons Act, and West Bengal's three registrations in 2021 show the route is used, but the same registration bias that depresses national counts limits what those figures show about incidence. Residents also live with the March 2026 recognition scheme and the 2024 removal of gender-identity-specific sexual-violence offences, both of which apply nationally.
outOfScopeNotes:
The outcome of the metro station FIR and of the counter-FIR filed by Metro Railway and the Railway Protection Force is unresolved in the sources; no disciplinary finding, charge or court decision is recorded.

The disposition of the South Dinajpur infiltration case is not sourced. Whether the charge proceeded, and whether the e-rickshaw driver and the arrested transgender person were convicted, deported or released, is unresolved.

Meeting frequency for West Bengal's own welfare board is not itemised. The sources give the national pattern of fewer than one meeting per year and the absence of a policy framework, but no West Bengal-specific attendance or budget figure.

The 2025 violence-prevalence survey is cited for its figures of 27.2% physical and 22.3% sexual violence; its sample, methodology and geographic coverage are not specified in the inventory and remain unresolved.

No West Bengal-specific court ruling, state policy on identity documents or markers, or state guidance on facilities is sourced. Whether West Bengal authorities have applied the March 2026 amendment's recognition categories in practice is not documented here.
